Latest Update: Balogun Wants to Join Man Utd, Ratcliffe Ready to Green Light Transfer

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Givemesport

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe is ready to green-light a striker deal in January to boost Mauricio Pochettino's squad, according to a report.
  • If Pochettino was in any way unaware of the challenge facing him at Old Trafford, he rapidly found out just 13 minutes into his first match in charge of Man United.
  • The 54-year-old would have been desperate to make a positive start to his Red Devils' reign, but instead his team were a man down and 2-0 behind just 13 minutes into his bow against Liverpool at Anfield.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe is ready to green-light a striker deal in January to boost Mauricio Pochettino's squad, according to a report.

If Pochettino was in any way unaware of the challenge facing him at Old Trafford, he rapidly found out just 13 minutes into his first match in charge of Man United.

The 54-year-old would have been desperate to make a positive start to his Red Devils' reign, but instead his team were a man down and 2-0 behind just 13 minutes into his bow against Liverpool at Anfield.

United's players did rally, but second half goals from Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz ensured they suffered a thrashing, leaving them 19th in the Premier League table.

Tottenham Hotspur picked up 18 points from their opening 11 matches last season and only avoided relegation to the Championship on the final day of the season, while United only have eight at the same stage.

They need to pick up their form quickly if they want to avoid being in a relegation battle themselves this term, and it appears as though club chiefs have decided that they need to invest in the January transfer window.

Having conceded more goals than any other team in Europe's top five leagues, it's clear that the defence needs to be a priority, with GIVEMESPORT sources revealing previously that they are looking at signing a centre-back and a striker in the winter market, as well as potentially a left-back.

The Times have now reported that signing a striker is the priority in January, with Benjamin Sesko set to be out until January, at least, having suffered a shin injury.

Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha have filled in this season in the Slovenian's absence, but neither have looked like they are going to score regularly there.

The report adds that United States star Folarin Balogun wants to reunite with Pochettino at Old Trafford, having worked with him at international level over the last two years.

United are unlikely to be able to go out and sign a top newly introduced striker in the mid-season winter market, so in that respect their options will be somewhat limited.

They will primarily be looking at centre-forwards who clubs are willing to sell or loan out, or strikers they will need to overpay for to bring to Old Trafford.

There have been some links to Ivan Toney and Victor Osimhen, who is said to be keen on the move, but both players are on huge salaries in Saudi Arabia and Turkey respectively, and would likely need to take wage cuts to move to Old Trafford.

The fact that United are in 19th position could also limit their options, especially if strikers don't want to make the move to Manchester to play for a club in crisis.

But Balogun, who has been described as 'insane' by teammate Christian Pulisic, could be a viable option for the Red Devils for many reasons, and a realistic signing.

Firstly, he wants to play for Pochettino, and he's clearly happy to do that for whatever club he is managing. So the 25-year-old would be ready to join United if it meant playing under the Argentine again.

In addition, Monaco are mentioned to be willing to sell the American because of their financial complications, and they came close to doing it in the summer window when Balogun was on the verge of joining Everton, after they agreed a £40m deal with the Ligue 1 outfit.

The Red Devils would probably ideally want to agree a loan deal with an option or obligation for Balogun in January, which would allow them to potentially spend on a newly introduced defender or two elsewhere, but it remains to be seen whether Monaco would be willing to agree to that.

However, completing a deal for the American appears to be one of their most straightforward options, so it will be interesting to see if they act on a transfer.

Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford?
  • Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.
  • After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

It has been revealed that goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

In a recent development, the second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Sources indicate that trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

Robin Roefs is at it again with another key save for Sunderland 👏 https://t.co/SJ4qWmSHBo.

Industry observers note that had the former Newcastle United player scored so late in the game, the home crowd’s frustration may have boiled over. The point means Le Bris’ side have still not won a league game since August and remain bottom of the table. This is proving to be a tougher second season in the top flight for Sunderland, but if they keep playing like this, they will not remain in the bottom three for much longer.

Sources indicate that “It’s a positive [point],” remarked Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”.

“It’s a positive [point], the more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.

“It’s still a long journey, we know with this busy schedule playing in Europe, playing in the Carabao Cup, it’s a new challenge for us and we need to embrace it. I think we showed this afternoon that we are in this challenge, we want to embrace it and be ourselves and we probably deserved a bit more today.”.

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Sunderland man remarked: “I think the wind played a big part and credit to both defences and the attacks as well to be able to keep it to no goals in that swirling wind.

“I think it was a good effort from everybody so obviously we want three points from where we are in the table but keep putting up the performances like that and we’ll get some.

“As a defender it’s always nice to have a clean sheet and especially after the last few games where we haven’t had one.

“It’s always something we’re looking to do and Robin [Roefs] came up with some massive saves, Omar [Alderete] coming on was really good as well and I hope my teammate’s [Nordi Mukiele] OK as well because I think that was kind of my fault. But we got the clean sheet for him so hopefully not too bad.”.

When asked about Sunderland being bottom of the league, he replied: “I think always the table reflects fairly where teams deserve to be, and I think over the course of the course of the season if we keep putting in performances like that it will represent where we should be.

“But the table always reflects where people should be but we need to keep looking at ourselves, don’t look at other anyone else, it’s no-one else’s fault but us and we know that.”.

That result means that Sunderland’s stay bottom of the Premier League and without a win in the competition since August 30, while Leeds earn their fifth draw in eight top-flight fixtures to move up to seventh on 11 points.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OLLIE LEWIS, SPORTS DIGITAL EDITOR and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 05:58 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 10:41 EST, 23 November 2026.

Mauricio Pochettino hauled his beleaguered Man United stars back into Carrington early on Monday morning after the latest manager's chastening Anfield bow on Sunday.

Pochettino, who replaced Michael Carrick last week, was served a sobering reality check at the hands of United's fierce rivals Liverpool, with the Red Devils on the receiving end of a 4-0 trouncing on Merseyside.

The Argentine bemoaned the impact of what he described as a harsh red card against defender Leny Yoro in the opening eight minutes of the contest, but admitted he has plenty to do to turn things around - with United stuck in 19th in the Premier League table.

And Pochettino had his players check in for training early on Monday morning, with a downcast Bruno Fernandes and his team-mates spotted arriving at around 8.30am - roughly an hour earlier than under Carrick.

Under Carrick's stewardship, players were given the day after a game off, and it remains to be seen whether Pochettino will do away with that approach in favour of a recovery day at the club's training ground - a similar approach to that taken by former United boss Ruben Amorim.

Man United stars were ordered back into training on Monday after their trouncing at Anfield.

Matthijs de Ligt cut a contemplative figure as he drove through the gates at Carrington.

Director of football Jason Wilcox continues to have questions to answer after Man United were unable to elevate themselves out of the relegation zone.

News also came on Monday that Man United are appealing to the FA over Yoro’s controversial red card.

Industry observers note that yoro was sent off in the eighth minute for a challenge on Alexander Isak on the edge of the penalty box. The Frenchman was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott, and Dominik Szoboszlai scored Liverpool’s first goal from the free kick as 10-man United were thrashed 4-0.

However, United insist that Yoro did not deny Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity because goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have reached the ball first.

The club have notified the FA of their intention to appeal in the hope of having Yoro’s one-match ban overturned so he can play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

In September, Pro Ref boss Howard Webb apologised to United when Erling Haaland’s winning goal for Manchester City in the Old Trafford derby was allowed to stand after VAR incorrectly ruled that teammate Enzo Fernandez was not interfering with play as he tried to head the ball in an offside position.

Last season, Webb acknowledged that the match officials got it wrong when they decided not to send off Brentford captain Nathan Collins for hauling back Bryan Mbeumo inside the box as United lost 3-1 at the Gtech Community Stadium.

New United head coach Pochettino blamed Yoro’s red card for the heavy defeat in his first game in charge, and was unhappy that Barrott took no action over a similar incident involving Jeremy Jacquet and Mbeumo in the Liverpool penalty area moments earlier.

'So painful, so disappointed,' remarked the Argentine. 'It's not OK to start a game in the Premier League with this situation. The game changed completely after eight minutes. Now we can explain everything, but the damage is done – it's so painful.

'It's clear that after eight minutes the blueprint was in the bin. Do you think that is easy? Even the best team in the world playing in this situation concedes four goals or maybe more.

'We are not going to lose more than one game how we lost today. I take the responsibility, and we keep pushing.

'We feel pain for this defeat, but we need to keep our heads up and translate that anger into energy to start to work from tomorrow for the next game.

Industry observers note that 'We are in a situation that this is very complicated. It's difficult, yes, but I think we fight, we made the effort, and I know how they feel now in the dressing-room.

'The players are feeling the pain of the result. I told them to be calm: it was an unfair situation that happened. We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.

'We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy.'.

But more critical were former Red Devils Roy Keane and Gary Neville, both of whom were pushed to extremes assessing the match after the final whistle.

Lisandro Martinez was among the Man United defenders that Gary Neville did not feel were up to the task at Anfield.

But incoming manager Pochettino was keen to place the majority of blame on the harsh red card doled out to Leny Yoro.

Neville was driven to slapping his face in the Sky Sports studio to demonstrate Man United's defenders' lack of hunger and poise.

'I never see any of them on their toes, alert, looking like they've got something fixed in here', he said before pointing to his head.

'I never see any of them look like that,' he added. 'They look like that -'.

Neville then stared into the middle distance for a few moments to share the blankness he sees on the faces of the back line, before spitting: 'Wake up!'.

The Overlap broadcaster slapped himself a number of times while repeating 'wake up!' and adding: 'You play for Man United'.

Keane was pushed to the brink of swearing in his snap description of the team's performance, adding that he thought Neville's verdict - that the 4-0 scoreline might have been worse under the circumstances - took players off the hook.

It has been revealed that 'If I hear that one more time from the lads in the commentary that 4-0 is not too bad when you're down to 10 men - has a team ever got a result with 10 men before?' Keane mentioned immediately after the final whistle. 'It can be done.

'I thought United were desperate. I thought they were so bad and everyone and Nev, who played for Man United saying 4-0 ain't bad.'.

Recent findings suggest that '(The red card) doesn't help but you're telling me they couldn't have done better? They lost 4-0 with 10 men, that's not too bad? Has a team ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality - I can't believe what I'm hearing from people.

'You played for the club, saying 4-0 isn't too bad. Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what? Performing rubbish. Liverpool were excellent, but how easy did United make it for them? I can't believe what I'm watching sometimes.

According to recent reports, 'This team two years ago finished 15th. The last year or two, we're talking. We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers.

'When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making? Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine, unbelievable chances they had. And everyone's coming off the pitch saying 4 is not too bad? I feel like swearing.'.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty.
  • According to recent reports, swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship.
  • Industry observers note that after sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty.

According to recent reports, swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship. On 14 November, he stayed up through the night completing the form and coordinating with referees across different time zones.

Industry observers note that after sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking. When he returned to submit it at around 8.50 p.m., applications had closed. The fellowship had reached its limit of 800 applications within 21 hours of opening.

It has been revealed that chowbey is not alone. Many researchers around the world found themselves unable to submit applications last Sunday and took to social media to vent their annoyance.

“It is incredibly frustrating to invest so much time and effort into developing a strong scientific project, only to discover that the timing of the application process may put some researchers at a disadvantage — especially when you open the system on Sunday and close it the same day,” wrote Ida Skubis, an AI researcher at Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice, Poland, on the social-media platform LinkedIn.

The Humboldt Research Fellowships support researchers from abroad to conduct research in Germany, providing €3,000 (US$3,300) a month for postdoctoral researchers and €3,600 a month for experienced researchers. Fellowships can last for 6–24 months for postdocs and 6–18 months for experienced researchers.

Recent findings suggest that the fellowships and awards are recognized internationally, which is why they are so competitive, claims Marcela Hernández, an environmental microbiologist at the University of Birmingham, UK, and a former fellow. “Being a Humboldtian is a mark of academic distinction. It has an exceptional international network.”.

A spokesperson for the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation in Bonn, Germany, mentioned in a statement to Nature that it had not anticipated that the application cap would be reached within 24 hours of opening. The foundation introduced the cap this year because it has seen a large increase in applications since 2024. It holds application rounds in March, July and November.

The spokesperson noted that as more researchers have used AI to help prepare their applications more quickly, the volume of applications has increased. Humboldt does not prohibit the use of generative AI in applications, nor are applicants required to declare AI use.

It has been revealed that simon Hammann, a chemist at the University of Hohenheim in Stuttgart, Germany, supported a research proposal as a prospective academic host for someone who was able to submit their application successfully. He states that opening the call on a Sunday disadvantaged researchers with family and caring responsibilities. “That should definitely be changed.”.

The Humboldt spokesperson said that the foundation advertises the date when applications will open, but that unfortunately the date fell on a Sunday this time.

Industry observers note that “We recognize the impact this had on those who were unable to apply, particularly given the challenges of coordinating availability over a weekend. We sincerely apologize for the disappointment and frustration this has caused,” the spokesperson remarked.

They added: “We will take this as an opportunity to continue reflecting on and improving our processes” to “find a transparent and fair solution”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
  • Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Sources indicate that virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas.".

Sources indicate that support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

In a recent development, particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it.".

Industry observers note that the debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:.

It has been revealed that in August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

Sources indicate that according to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

Sources indicate that but how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she mentioned in an interview with DW.

Industry observers note that neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?".

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

Industry observers note that DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization.".

Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

In a recent development, * Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.

What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

📅 05 Oct 2022 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios revealed on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.
  • This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.
  • The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios revealed on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival.".

Recent findings suggest that based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​.

It has been revealed that the first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

Recent findings suggest that in the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond.".

In a recent development, shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their aims.

According to recent reports, although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

According to recent reports, certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Sources indicate that aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

In a recent development, smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

Sources indicate that one can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

It has been revealed that his pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral.".

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

It has been revealed that in the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary.".

Recent findings suggest that in the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian.".

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

It has been revealed that now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17.".

According to recent reports, pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scoring from 12 yards isn’t as easy as it looks with some of the best football players in the history of the sport guilty of missing many penalties. Despite this, there are some very good penalty takers in the modern game who are able to block out the noise and pick their spot.

Industry observers note that typically, every team has a designated spot-kick taker and this player will be able to thrive under pressure and have an accurate ball-striking technique. However, even the most consistent penalty-kick takers can be prone to the occasional error, with goalkeepers such as Emi Martinez being known for his ability to save penalties.

On this list of the players with the most penalties missed, there are some surprising inclusions, such as spot-kick expert Cristiano Ronaldo, who ranks highly. With that in mind, here are the 12 players who have missed the most penalties in the 21st century.

Misses in penalty shootouts have not been counted in the individual tallies. And if two players are level on the number of penalty misses, then the player who has the worst conversion rate will rank higher.

The Argentine had a 77.4% conversion rate from penalties, which is far from being considered poor. However, this number is inflated due to the sheer number of penalties that the striker took. He scored 48 during his illustrious career and missed 14.

Sources indicate that aguero will be remembered for his pathetic penalty attempt in his final appearance for Manchester City. The talented forward tried an audacious panenka, which was caught with ease by Chelsea goalkeeper Edouard Mendy. This was a costly miss too, as in the second half Chelsea came from behind to win the Premier League encounter 2-1 in the dying moments.

Veteran Antonio Di Natale had a wonderful career and will be remembered more for his impressive performances in Serie A rather than his penalty misses. He won the Serie A top goalscorer award in 2010 and he also won the Serie A Italian Footballer of the Year award in the same year.

One year later he reclaimed the top goalscorer award after another brilliant league campaign. The lethal finisher retired in 2016 as Udinese’s all-time top scorer with 227 goals to his name. Out of the 44 spot-kicks Di Natale took, he missed just 14, giving him a 75.8% conversion rate.

Harry Kane is in the conversation when you think of the greatest penalty takers of all time. The Englishman is usually ice-cold from 12 yards, often smashing the ball into the corners with power and pinpoint accuracy. He has a mightily impressive 87.5% conversion rate, the highest of any player on this list, having scored 115 of his 131 attempts.

For his current club, Bayern Munich, he has scored 42 of his 46 attempts from 12 yards, while for England, he has been successful with 28 of his 33 spot-kicks.

He isn't automatic from 12 yards, though. Of his 16 missed spot-kicks, his most famous came in England's defeat to France in the 2022 World Cup. He had the opportunity to equalise late in the quarter-final tie, but Kane blazed his effort over the bar, with England eventually losing 2-1. He also missed his first effort from 12 yards directly after winning the 2026 Ballon d'Or, hitting the bar against Borussia Dortmund that same week.

Industry observers note that the striker has missed 16 penalties since 2001 and, despite a somewhat solid 79.7% conversion rate from the spot, he is in the top ten for most missed penalties in the 21st century. The Uruguayan was Napoli’s primary penalty taker, and although he scored the majority of his spot kicks for the Italian side, he did miss some crucial ones too.

Cavani, known for his poacher-like qualities, was never the designated penalty taker at Paris Saint-Germain. The 39-year-old had competition from world-class superstars such as Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Neymar in the early stints of his spell in France and this was before Kylian Mbappe had arrived in the French capital.

Likewise, at Manchester United, Cavani never took a penalty outside a shootout, and this was because of the presence of Cristiano Ronaldo, Bruno Fernandes, Anthony Martial and Marcus Rashford, who were all ahead of him in the spot-kick pecking order.

At his final club, Boca Juniors, he scored three of his five attempts from 12 yards.

Generally, you wouldn’t associate penalties with the former Barcelona and AC Milan man, but he was clearly trusted from the penalty spot.

Recent findings suggest that ronaldinho did in fact miss 16 penalties. However, three of these spot-kicks were taken before 2001 and therefore aren't included in this ranking. Despite converting most of his penalties, the ambitious playmaker made a name for himself for taking free kicks. Ronaldinho would often deploy an unusual but effective strategy, which entailed striking the ball underneath the wall rather than over or around it.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic is a player who loves being in the spotlight. The Swede has scored some of the best goals in the most pressured situations, winning cups and leagues for a variety of different teams.

According to recent reports, with that being noted, Ibrahimovic took it upon himself to take penalties throughout his career and he stepped up to take 104 penalties. Despite this, the pressure of taking a penalty gets to even the best players at times and therefore his 17 penalty misses are more than understandable. Ibrahimovic, who retired at the age of 41, scored 87 goals from the penalty spot at an 83.6% conversion rate.

For as incredible as Kylian Mbappe is in front of goal, the fact he has missed from 12 yards on 17 occasions throughout his career is a huge surprise. His latest miss came when his spot-kick in Real Madrid's La Liga clash against Celta in November 2026 ballooned well over the bar.

He will go down as one of the greatest goalscorers of all time, and maybe the fact he's trusted with penalty efforts for both club and country means he's bound to miss a fair few more than others around him.

Francesco Totti will go down as one of the best penalty-takers in the 21st century, yet he finds himself ranked highly on the list too. The striker scored so many goals during his playing days and, as expected, he has a conversion rate above 80%.

Amazingly, Totti didn’t miss a single penalty during his final four and a half seasons, converting 13 consecutive penalties at the back end of his career. The Italian did miss another two penalties in his career, but this was in 2001 and is therefore not counted in his tally. The versatile forward spent his entire career at Roma, winning the Serie A title, two Coppa Italia and two Supercoppa Italiana titles.

Immobile is best known for his spell at Lazio, where he holds the record as the club’s all-time top goalscorer. Furthermore, he also sits eighth on the all-time list of Serie A top goalscorers, which is another significant accomplishment for the striker.

The Italian missed 19 penalties in his career, which gives him an 81.9% conversion rate from 12 yards out. In August 2026, he decided to retire, so he won't have to worry about climbing any further up this list.

According to recent reports, neymar has stepped up to take penalties for club and country throughout his career and he has never shied away from this kind of pressure. The flamboyant winger will go down as one of the best takers of the modern generation, despite missing 22 penalties so far in his career.

Neymar has a slow run-up and typically goes for placement over power. The Brazilian has scored 97 penalties, which gives him a very respectable 81.5% conversion rate from the penalty spot. The 34-year-old has been the primary penalty taker for Paris Saint-Germain, Santos and the Brazil national team, while he took fewer penalties at Barcelona due to Lionel Messi being the main taker.

There could also be a return to the starting line-up for summer signing Trevoh Chalobah following his recent return from injury, while Maximo Perrone could replace Samuele Ricci in midfield.

Como’s biggest injury news is that Italy international Moise Kean is set to spend another few months on the sidelines after suffering a setback in his return from an injury that has already kept him out of action for the last five weeks.

AEK are expected to turn to former Milan and Fiorentina striker Luka Jovic to lead their attack at the Stadio Sinigaglia on Tuesday night.

Como (4-2-3-1): Butez; Couto, Ramon, Chalobah, Valle; Perrone, Milla; Da Cunha, Paz, Baturina; Douvikas.

AEK (4-4-2): Strakosha; Rota, Moukoudi, Relvas, Pilos; Majer, Marin, Vitalis, Kutesa; Jovic, Gacinovic.

Ian Holloway has been sacked by Swindon just two days after attempting to confront angry fans following defeat to Newport on Saturday.

The journeyman manager had himself called the 2-0 loss on the road 'unforgivable' after he was taunted by home supporters chanting that he would be 'sacked in the morning' after the result.

Holloway had intended to go down the tunnel after the final whistle, and passed the away stand on his route out, taking off his cap as he held up his hands in resignation.

But as boos rained down on him, the 63-year-old could not resist the urge to engage, looking to answer back to the fans before he was restrained by security.

Last month, Holloway described himself as a 'dead man walking' with the Robins mired 17th in League Two, but Monday morning saw him despatched after two seasons in charge.

'Since joining the club towards the end of 2024, Ian has played an vital role in stabilising our on-field position and helping the club make progress season upon season,' the Swindon statement announcing his departure read.

Saturdays eh.#STFC pic.twitter.com/1GL3blApwW.

Ian Holloway was caught up in a clash with fans after Swindon's defeat to Newport County - shortly before he was sacked (Source: X/Loathed Stranger).

The journeyman manager oversaw two seasons at the club, saving them from relegation in 2024-25.

'However, following careful consideration of recent results and performances, the club believes that now is the right time to take a different direction.

'This has not been an easy decision, but the board firmly believes that it is crucial to make difficult decisions when necessary, always with the best interests of Swindon Town at heart.'.

Holloway cut a disillusioned figure at Rodney Parade as he gave a heartfelt assessment of his side's performance after defeat to the Exiles.

'It's devastating,' noted Holloway. 'I'm bitterly disappointed. Did I expect my team to do that? Not in a million years.

'We're getting regular mistakes from almost everyone in that backline and in that midfield. We knew what type of game it was going to be. There's no excuses. I've just remarked to them "what on Earth do you think you're doing?" To start that way? It was so passive it was unforgivable.

'It's very painful at the minute. It'll come back at the manager in the end if I listen to all these people (from the stands).

'This is football. I've been in it a long time. This is my life.'.

Holloway also questioned the desire of his players, continuing: 'Bitterly disappointed in all of them and disappointed for the fans. I get it, that didn't look like our team.

Industry observers note that 'They scored two ugly goals. All our chances that we had, normally we take them.

'Where's the fight? It's a local derby. I'm sorry, they've done their bits better than us.'.

Holloway has endured an uneven stint at Swindon since 2024, saving the club from relegation in his first season but failing to challenge for the promotion places as time wore on.

Memorably, the former Crystal Palace and Queen's Park Rangers manager claimed that the training ground was haunted shortly after his arrival in Wiltshire.

Holloway had first suggested that there had been 'some strange things happening' after the club captain Ollie Clarke had ruptured his ankle in training, before enlisting his wife Kim to free spirits potentially trapped in the South West.

'I'm absolutely devastated so I'm going to try and cleanse the training ground area because people are telling me it's haunted,' Holloway said on BBC Radio Wiltshire in November 2024.

Industry observers note that 'There's a graveyard somewhere near. Honestly, I'm not joking.

'I think our training ground is very close to an ancient burial site so I'm going to get my wife to come up and say sorry to all these people and hopefully we'll have a bit more luck.'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Sources indicate that imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft rolled out almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

Sources indicate that when Voyager 1 released, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

Recent findings suggest that it flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Industry observers note that its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," notes Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Industry observers note that but you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

It has been revealed that the spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

By ISABEL BALDWIN, US ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 10:23 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 13:19 EST, 23 November 2026.

The World Cup is set to return to America after FIFA awarded the 2031 women's tournament to a historic four-nation bid.

Following the success of the men's tournament this summer, the United States was confirmed as one of the hosts of the women's edition in five years' time during a virtual meeting of FIFA's national associations on Monday.

The US will co-host the global soccer extravaganza alongside Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica after the four countries' joint bid was awarded uncontested the 2031 tournament.

The selection marks a milestone for the Women's World Cup with the tournament being hosted across four nations for the first time in its history.

The last World Cup was co-hosted by multiple countries for the first time with the 2023 edition taking place across Australia and New Zealand.

This summer's men's World Cup was also co-hosted by the US with games taking place across the States, Canada and Mexico.

The World Cup is set to return to the United States for the 2031 women's edition of the event.

Spain are reigning champions after winning the Women's World Cup in 2023.

The United States Women's National Team are four-time winners in 1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019.

The 2031 tournament will also be the largest in the competition's history, featuring an expanded 48-team field and 104 matches for the first time.

'We are incredibly honored and excited to welcome the world to the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica for the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup,' said US Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone.

'This is a historic moment for our four countries, but the opportunity is much bigger than any one of us. Together with FIFA, we want to deliver the biggest and most impactful Women's World Cup in history and use its success to accelerate the growth of women's soccer around the world. Our ambition is to create a tournament that not only inspires millions of players, but helps give them the opportunities to play, grow and pursue their dreams.'.

According to recent reports, the selection marks the third time that the Women's World Cup has been awarded to the US with the country previously hosting the landmark 1999 and 2003 editions alone. The national team's tournament win in 1999 was the second of its four titles.

Meanwhile, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will become first-time hosts at the historic tournament.

'This milestone furthers the continued belief that the best days of soccer in America are still ahead,' mentioned U.S. Soccer CEO and General Secretary JT Batson.

'We have an opportunity to use the momentum from the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup to accelerate our ambitions for the future of soccer, from expanding access and participation to strengthening the pathways that develop the next generation of players. We are excited to work alongside our partners across the region to make this tournament a defining moment for women's soccer.'.

The U.S.-led 2031 project across the CONCACAF regional soccer body bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

US Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone said the federation was honored to be selected.

The host selection of the 2035 Women's World Cup was awarded to a joint bid between England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

The host selection of the 2035 Women's World Cup was also announced on Monday with the tournament being awarded to another joint bid between England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

It marks the first time that a World Cup has been hosted on the British Isles since the men's tournament in 1966 in England.

The United Kingdom bid joins England with Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales that offers a choice from 19 venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments - the first editions with 48 teams and 104 games - and to reinvest all that money in women's soccer.

Industry observers note that FIFA wanted these heavyweights of women's soccer to face no opposition without rival bids and so lead hosting the first expanded tournaments. That will bring parity with the men's World Cup which expanded to 48 teams this year in the US, Canada and Mexico.

The 2027 Women's World Cup will have 32 teams in Brazil.

‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did.
  • According to recent reports, to err is human, science endeavours included.
  • Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did. Credit: Igor Andreoni/Peter Shawhan.

According to recent reports, to err is human, science endeavours included. Accounts of missteps in the laboratory or field abound among early-career researchers, as do tales of what they learnt from them. But senior scientists make mistakes, too — and not just early in their careers.

Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem. Other times, graduate students saved their advisers from throwing away ‘wrong’ data. Senior scientists also know the dangers of overthinking and how it can lead to experimental paralysis. “Every year, I devote a meeting with students and postdocs to discuss failures and how errors of judgement or methods are part of academic life,” says Catherine Badgley, a palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. “I hope this helps them to see they can learn from mistakes rather than be devastated by them.”.

Nature’s careers team spoke to Badgley and four other senior scientists to hear about their ‘failures’ and the lessons they took from them.

Physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park and a deputy spokesperson for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) scientific collaboration.

Recent findings suggest that for the past 26 years, I have been searching for gravitational waves with LIGO, which has a gravitational-wave observatory in Livingston, Louisiana. These waves are echoes of massive events such as the merging of black holes or the collision of neutron stars. They produce ripples in space-time and, by the time these tiny ripples reach Earth, they are so faint that scientists need extra help to ‘hear’ them, because they are extremely hard to detect by just using light, or telescopes, to see them. For example, observations of a collision of two neutron stars with telescopes has revealed the presence of gold and platinum atoms, solving a long-standing question: what is the origin of about half of all elements heavier than iron? The detection of such an event with LIGO would get us even more information.

Industry observers note that in the first tests of LIGO, the team found nothing. Later, with improved detectors, we still found nothing.

Industry observers note that in fact, we got very good at reporting nothing. We became experienced with knowing what we could rule out. By the time we made our first wave detection, in 2015, a finding that earned LIGO founders a physics Nobel in 2017, we had published about 100 papers reporting null results.

One such null case was in 2010. We were completing a science run, in which data are collected for a set period of time, and had a candidate for a striking event — it looked like we’d finally got there. But we knew it might be a ‘blind injection’, which is when a false signal is inserted into a data set by authorized colleagues to test our analyses.

It has been revealed that we finished the analysis, drafted the paper and then asked the LIGO director to open a sealed envelope to tell us whether this was a real event or not. It wasn’t, but the exercise highlighted a real problem: the sky location our analysis recovered didn’t match the signal’s known location. Two of the detector’s mirrors had moved in the wrong direction. We found the glitch in about a day. This showed we could efficiently self-correct when detecting a real sign — which happened five years later.

In a recent development, I tell my students that scientists make lots of mistakes. We’re careful with cross-checks and analyse results carefully, so we catch almost all of them. Some are caught in minutes, some in days and some take more work. This one, because we’d built a test designed to assess itself, took about a day. That’s really the goal: not avoiding mistakes, but rather building enough ways to catch them swiftly. Knowing what it means to find nothing is crucial; it’s a real scientific skill.

Chemist Omar Yaghi (second row, fifth from right), with his team at Tsinghua University in Beijing, says that professors can learn key lessons from their students if they listen to them.Credit: Yaghi Group Photo.

Chemist at Tsinghua University in Beijing and a co-recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work with metal–organic frameworks.

Back in the 1990s, I was an assistant professor at Arizona State University in Tempe. My team had begun research trying to make inorganic porous materials. These are solid materials with a network of tiny, connected pores that act like molecular sponges to trap molecules, such as wastewater contaminants and toxic gases, on their surfaces. We were successful: we had a paper1 published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society and, later, in Science2.

Then a doctoral student came looking to join my lab. She didn’t sound very confident, her English was not so good and it wasn’t the right time of year to look for a PhD adviser. I made up some reason not to take her. But she kept coming back and was adamant about working with me.

So I accepted her into my lab group, and she started working on metal–organic compounds, another type of porous material. I felt that this was a waste of time: researchers had known about these structures since the 1950s, but nothing useful had resulted from them. Once you emptied their solvent-filled pores to trap other molecules, such as gases, they collapsed and became useless. I used to call them sculptures: they had beauty, but no function.

She kept at it, and I held onto my scepticism. After a year, we sat down to discuss her results. That was when I realized that there was an opportunity there: we could make robust metal–organic compounds, after all.

Sources indicate that metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are also materials full of tiny pores. But what makes them particularly interesting is that scientists can adjust the size and shape of those pores, as well as the chemical properties inside them. This makes MOFs more tunable than inorganic porous materials such as zeolites and much better at trapping some gases. Some MOFs can drive chemical reactions, some conduct electricity and some are stable enough to be reused.

Industry observers note that my student found strong chemical bindings that gave stability to early versions of these structures and, within a very short period, our findings were published in Nature3. It had worked.

Decades later, I met with my former student, and she told me that she had been struggling back then and wanted to try her luck with me, a new professor at the time, because no one else would take her in.

I think science is the greatest equalizer. One discovery can take you from humble beginnings, as it did for us, and propel you to the top of your profession.

In a recent development, I had an opinion about an area of research and didn’t listen to my student, and, to that student’s credit, she persisted. To my credit, I changed my thinking. Neither the student nor the professor can afford to do science without the other.

Plant geneticist Chris Martine’s misidentified sample led to the identification of a upcoming species of bush tomato plant in northern Australia. Credit: Jason Cantley.

Plant geneticist at Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and president of the Botanical Society of America.

I’ve studied Australia’s bush tomatoes for about 25 years. My team was the first to describe Solanum ossicruentum, nicknamed the blood bone tomato because it seems to bleed when cut open. It got us some press coverage and was a major deal for our laboratory in 20164.

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, Angela McDonnell, a postdoc, joined us. We started a significant genetics project to build an evolutionary tree to understand the family history of the bush tomatoes we had been studying for years. We had two samples of S. ossicruentum from two locations: the Tanami Desert and the Keep River National Park, both in northern Australia. When the results of testing came back, genomic differences landed them in totally different places on the evolutionary tree of the group.

Industry observers note that in my mind, there was no way it was possible. I’d identified the specimens myself. I assumed we’d mislabelled something. I asked Angela to check everything carefully, but she was certain that wasn’t the case. To me it didn’t add up — I came close to saying, “let’s just pull the misplaced one and call it an error”.

Sources indicate that two years ago, while looking through the folders of S. ossicruentum specimens at the Northern Territory Herbarium in Palmerston, Australia, I noticed some that had strange dots on the backs of their leaves. At first, I thought it was mildew, but then I wondered whether these dots were extrafloral nectaries, or nectar-producing glands found outside the plant’s flower. Then I realized the plants with such dots were mostly from one part of Australia, the northern edge of the Tanami Desert — exactly where I was heading next.

In a recent development, when I got there, plants with these little dots were dripping with nectar with ants harvesting it, an interaction I hadn’t seen to this level before. I checked whether Angela’s significant phylogeny project had anything from that region, and there it was — the misplaced plant. The two samples of what I thought were S. ossicruentum belonged in two different places on the evolutionary tree because they were two different species. Indeed, that initial sample’s evolutionary tree placement was the best evidence for the newly introduced species that we later described: Solanum nectarifolium5. My first thought was to thank Angela for not pulling that specimen out of our analysis. I was honestly thrilled.

Before that, I had felt overconfident in what I knew, and Angela was certain that this was a carefully curated data set and a rigorously achieved genetic result. As I’ve become more senior, I’ve become more comfortable with uncertainty: when something doesn’t fit our preconceived ideas, that’s an interesting result — that’s how you find more new things.

Now I realize how crucial it is for people who are more junior than myself to speak up and share their ideas, especially when they run counter to convention. If we look back at the history of science, that’s the only way we’ve progressed.

Palaeontologist Catherine Badgley notes that a key skill for scientists is knowing when to stop pursuing a good idea that simply isn’t working. Credit: David Bay.

Palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.

In the 1990s, I was an associate research scientist in the University of Michigan’s Museum of Paleontology. Serge Legendre, a colleague who was then at the University of Montpellier in France, highlighted me a new way, at the time, of explaining body-size distributions in fossils of extinct mammalian species. He used cenograms — a graphical technique that ranks mammalian species in a community by body size.

Industry observers note that in well-watered ecosystems, there was a fairly continuous line: all species were closely spaced in size. But habitats with long dry seasons had a significant gap in the middle where medium-sized mammals would be — an interesting mystery. Legendre found that many animals in that size range are fruit-eaters, and fruit isn’t available in arid or very cold environments all year long. If the theory was correct, we might be able to infer past climate from the sizes of mammals in fossil communities.

I had a lot of climate data for mammal locations worldwide, so the two of us, as well as palaeontologist Philip Gingerich, who was then also at the University of Michigan, decided to build a much larger database of locations and add climate variables. We wanted to determine whether climate variables could predict the size gap we saw. I was excited enough that I wrote it up as a book proposal and received a contract from the University of Chicago Press.

Recent findings suggest that but the more data that we collected, the fuzzier the picture became. After more than a year, I had written four chapters. But I had to admit we had fewer results than when we started.

I knew the data weren’t flawed because I had used this enormous mammalian fossil database successfully for other research projects. For example, undergraduate students used it to show that the length of the growing season, as a climate variable, could be used to predict the number of fruit- and plant-eating species at a given time.

I eventually realized that each continent has its own evolutionary history and its own climatic circumstances — no one is exactly like another. Our largest data sets, from Africa and North America, have almost completely non-overlapping climates, so one was never going to be a good model for predicting the other.

A League Two footballer has been charged with rape and remanded into custody, following a hearing at Hatfield Magistrates' Court.

Isiah Noel-Williams, who plays his football for League Two side Barnet, was arrested and appeared in court on Saturday, charged with three counts of rape, as well as sexual communication with a child.

The midfielder, who has made seven appearances for the Bees this season, joined the EFL side from non-league outfit Hemel Hempstead Town in the summer, having spent the entirety of his career to that point playing in non-league.

The 23-year-old was part of the Hemel Hempstead team that took Wigan Athletic all the way to a penalty shootout in the FA Cup first round last season, with the team also suffering penalty shootout heartbreak in the National League South play-off quarter-final, beaten by Weston-super-Mare 5-4 on spot-kicks.

In a statement, Hertfordshire Police remarked: "Isiah Noel-Williams, aged 23 and of High Oaks, St Albans, has been charged with three counts of rape, one count of assault by penetration, one count of engaging in sexual communication with a child, and one count of supplying a controlled drug (Class B), following an investigation by Hertfordshire Constabulary’s Public Protection Command.

Recent findings suggest that "Noel-Williams appeared at Hatfield Magistrates’ Court on Saturday, November 21, where he was remanded into custody. He will next appear at St Albans Crown Court on Tuesday, December 22.".

Noel-Williams is the son of former Watford, Brighton and Stoke player Gifton Noel-Williams, who played in the Premier League and Championship during a 13-year career.

In a statement, his club Barnet said: "Barnet FC can confirm that first-team player Isiah Noel-Williams has been charged and remanded in custody as part of a police investigation by Hertfordshire Constabulary.

Sources indicate that "The club is co-operating fully with the authorities and will determine any further action in due course. As this is now a matter for the courts, the club will not be making any further comment.".

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

It has been revealed that united enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

Sources indicate that in stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Industry observers note that bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.
